summary: Describes how to carry real-time text conversation content, as specified in ITU-T T.140, in RTP packets alongside audio within one RTP session. It recommends including redundant copies of recently sent text to reduce the risk of loss when packets are dropped. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: Like a phone call that also sends typed chat letters. Each packet repeats the last few letters in case one packet gets lost.

questions: how to send text over rtp
subtitle: Sending typed messages during voice calls over RTP.

tldr.problem: Real-time text conversations need to be sent alongside voice in multimedia sessions, but must arrive in order, without duplication, and with detectable loss.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4351 defines the audio/t140c RTP payload format to carry T.140 text characters with a counter for sequencing and optional redundant copies to reduce loss.
tldr.outcome: This allows PSTN gateways and multimedia applications to transmit text interleaved with audio in a single RTP session, though it is now historic.

today: RFC 4351 is Historic and is not recommended for new implementations. Applications that need real-time text should use RFC 4103 instead. This RFC documents the original audio/t140c format used in some deployed PSTN gateways.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
T.140 real-time text is text transmitted character-by-character as it is typed, at a rate of a few characters per second. RFC 4351 defines how to carry T.140 text in RTP packets alongside audio within a single RTP session. This enables multimedia conversation services that combine voice, video, and text on the same stream, such as PSTN gateways connecting textphone users over IP networks.

T.140 specifies that text must be transmitted in UTF-8 encoding, and the receiving system must deliver text without loss, duplication, or reordering. Packet loss in RTP is common, so the RFC includes mechanisms for detecting lost text and for sending redundant copies of recent characters to recover from loss.
sections.eli5: This explains how to send text over RTP, the same protocol used for voice calls. Text arrives character by character, just like you are typing it.

sections.title: The audio/t140c Payload Format
sections.content:
The RFC defines the audio/t140c MIME type for text inside audio streams. Each RTP packet payload consists of a 16-bit T140block counter followed by one T140block (the actual T.140 text data). The counter starts at 1 and increments with each packet to detect lost blocks and prevent duplication. The counter wraps back to 1 after reaching 65535.

Most packets carry a single UTF-8 encoded character or a small block of text. The first packet in a session and the first packet after an idle period set the RTP marker bit to signal a new conversation or resumption.
sections.eli5: Each message has a number (starting at 1) so the receiver can spot if any messages are missing. The text itself is just UTF-8 characters, usually one or a few per packet.

sections.title: Protection Against Loss
sections.content:
Since text in real-time conversations must arrive reliably, the RFC recommends redundancy based on RFC 2198: the transmitter sends the current text plus redundant copies of one or two previous blocks. The redundant blocks include their own T140block counters so the receiver can match them to missing primary blocks.

When there is an idle period (no new text for more than 300 milliseconds), the sender transmits an empty T140block to signal the end of that batch, and continues sending the previous non-empty block as redundant data until all redundancy levels have been transmitted.
sections.eli5: The trick to keeping text from getting lost is to send each letter multiple times, spaced out in different packets. If one packet disappears, an earlier or later copy usually arrives.

sections.title: Examples and Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC provides examples of RTP packets with and without redundancy, showing the packet headers and payload layout. It also defines the cps parameter (characters per second) in SDP, which allows a receiver to request that the sender limit the text rate. The default is 30 characters per second, averaged over any 10-second window.

SDP examples show how to set up a session with G.711 audio and text at 6 characters per second, or with two levels of redundancy at 20 characters per second.
sections.eli5: You can tell the other side how fast you want text to arrive, and the packets show which parts are new text and which are safety copies.

sections.title: Security and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC notes that text in a conversation is sensitive and should be encrypted, using SRTP (Secure RTP) where available. It also warns that automated systems must not send text faster than a human user could type, to avoid congestion. The recommended buffering time is 300 milliseconds, and if the network is congested the sender should increase buffering time or reduce the character rate rather than reducing redundancy.

The audio/t140c format is intended only for PSTN gateway applications that need to conserve RTP sessions. General real-time text applications should use RFC 4103 instead.
sections.eli5: Keep text encrypted, do not flood the network with text, and send extra copies to keep conversation flowing even if the network is dropping packets.
